\section[\texorpdfstring{\te{తీయని} (tīyani)}{తీయని (tīyani)}]{\te{తీయని} (tīyani) — sweet (of taste)}

\label{lesson:TE-C141-tiyani}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Telugu for golden, then the Telugu for spoiled.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{తీయని}}
\textbf{\te{తీయని}} — \emph{tīyani} — \textquotedblleft{}sweet (of taste)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{తీయని}} (\emph{tīyani}) is native Dravidian, one word with Tamil \emph{tīm}, \textquotedblleft{}sweet\textquotedblright{} (DEDR 3268), which lists Telugu \emph{tiyyani}, \textquotedblleft{}sweet\textquotedblright{}. DEDR compares, with a query, Prakrit \emph{tiṇisa}, \textquotedblleft{}honeycomb\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{tīyani}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{tīyani}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Telugu for golden, then the Telugu for spoiled, then say \emph{tīyani} again
\end{itemize}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\te{చేదైన} (cēdaina)}{చేదైన (cēdaina)}]{\te{చేదైన} (cēdaina) — bitter-tasting}

\label{lesson:TE-C141-cedaina}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Telugu for spoiled, then the Telugu for sweet.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{చేదైన}}
\textbf{\te{చేదైన}} — \emph{cēdaina} — \textquotedblleft{}bitter-tasting\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{చేదైన}} (\emph{cēdaina}) is native Dravidian: \emph{cēdu}, \textquotedblleft{}bitter\textquotedblright{} (DEDR 1249), and \emph{ayina}, \textquotedblleft{}which is\textquotedblright{} (DEDR 333). DEDR compares Sanskrit \emph{kaṣāya}, \textquotedblleft{}astringent\textquotedblright{}, with \emph{cēdu}.
\end{cousinweb}
